screens.title: Interfaces: Defining Contracts
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we treat interfaces as formal contracts that describe what an object can do, not how it stores state. You'll learn how to declare an interface with the interface keyword and make classes adhere to that contract using implements. We'll look at how interfaces let a class belong to multiple type hierarchies, why that matters for loose coupling, and how Java 8 introduced default and static methods so interfaces can evolve safely. You will see concrete code examples: Flyable and Swimmable, a Duck class implementing both, and an Airplane implementing only Flyable. We'll also contrast interfaces with abstract classes so you can choose the right tool when designing systems. By the end you will understand when to define behaviors as interfaces, how default methods preserve compatibility, and how static interface methods offer utility behavior. Think of an interface as a promise: a class that signs it guarantees certain behaviors. Keep that promise clear and focused, and your codebase stays modular and easy to change.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Interfaces: Defining Contracts
Interfaces: Defining Contracts
A contract for behavior: what an object can do, independent of state.

Interfaces let you declare method signatures and constants. Classes that implement an interface promise to provide those behaviors. With Java 8, interfaces can include default implementations and static utilities so contracts can evolve without breaking implementers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives guide what you will practice and why it matters. First, you'll be able to explain what an interface is in Java and how it acts as a contract for classes: that definition helps you design clear APIs and reason about capability-based types. Second, you'll use the interface keyword and implements clause to write interfaces and make concrete classes adhere to them; this skill is essential for building modular code and testing via mock implementations. Third, you'll distinguish interfaces from abstract classes: when to prefer behavior-focused interfaces versus inheritance-backed abstract classes that may carry shared state. Fourth, you will implement Java 8 features: default methods and static methods in interfaces, understanding how default methods allow you to evolve APIs without breaking existing implementers. Each objective ties directly to writing clearer, loosely coupled code that is easier to extend and maintain. Practice these in small examples and the printable-document activity to confirm mastery.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Benefits
screens.narratorSegment: This second set of objectives focuses on applying interfaces in design and practice. You will build example classes that implement multiple interfaces, demonstrating multiple inheritance of type and how it enables polymorphism: a method can accept any object that satisfies an interface, regardless of its concrete class. You will implement default and static methods in interfaces and observe how a default method can be overridden when a class needs specialized behavior. You will practice the printable-document activity: define Printable, implement Report and Invoice, and iterate through an array of Printable objects to print polymorphically. Finally, you'll learn why interfaces promote loose coupling: code depends on capability types rather than concrete implementations, simplifying testing and extension. Each objective connects to writing maintainable, extensible systems where behavior is explicit and substitutable. screens.title: What is an Interface?
screens.narratorSegment: An interface is a contract: it declares a set of method signatures that a class promises to implement. Unlike classes, interfaces are about behavior — 'can-do' — not about how data is stored. Historically, interfaces contained only abstract method signatures and public static final constants. That meant interfaces described what actions existed without any implementation detail. Understanding this distinction is crucial: when you design APIs, use interfaces to express capabilities other parts of your code can rely on, rather than tying them to a concrete implementation. A concrete example is a Flyable interface with void fly(). Any class—Duck, Airplane, Drone—that implements Flyable guarantees it can fly, and code can accept Flyable parameters without caring about the class behind it. A common misconception is to use interfaces to share state; interfaces do not hold instance state. If you need shared state or a partial implementation with fields, an abstract class may be appropriate. Takeaway: interfaces make behavior explicit and interchangeable; they simplify testing and extension by allowing substitution based on capability alone. Can you spot where a behavior belongs to an interface versus to a class with state?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: An interface defines behaviors (method signatures) a class must implement; it represents a promise, not shared instance state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What is an Interface?
Interface as a Contract
Behavior-focused, no instance state
• An interface lists method signatures that must be implemented by classes that adopt it.
• It expresses capability: a class that implements Flyable can be used anywhere Flyable is required.
• Interfaces promote loose coupling by letting code depend on the interface type instead of concrete classes.
• Misconception: interfaces are not substitutes for shared state; use abstract classes when you need common fields or constructor logic.
Analogy
Think of an interface as a job description: it lists responsibilities but not the employee's personal data.
Key Takeaway
Use interfaces to make behaviors explicit, substitutable, and testable without sharing instance state.
Example
// Interface for objects that can fly
interface Flyable {
  void fly();
}

// A class promises to implement fly()
class Airplane implements Flyable {
  String model;
  public Airplane(String model) { this.model = model; }
  @Override
  public void fly() {
    System.out.println(model + " is soaring through the sky!");
  }
}
Check
Does the class expose state needed by other components, or only behavior? If only behavior, prefer an interface.

screens.title: Declaring Interfaces and Implementing Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through how to declare an interface and make a class implement it. You use the interface keyword followed by method signatures. Implementing classes use implements and must provide concrete implementations for each abstract method. This pattern enables compile-time guarantees about available behaviors. As a concrete example, the Flyable interface declares void fly() and a default takeOff() in Java 8. A Duck class implements Flyable and Swimmable and supplies fly() and swim() method bodies; it can also override the default takeOff() to provide a specialized startup behavior. Note that fields declared in interfaces are implicitly public static final, so interfaces are not a place to put mutable instance fields. A common mistake is forgetting to add @Override annotations for implemented methods; while optional, they help catch signature mismatches at compile time. Practically, declare small focused interfaces for single responsibilities. Below you will find a code panel showing an interface, a class that implements it, and small runtime output to illustrate behavior. Use this pattern to document capabilities and enable polymorphic APIs that accept interface types rather than concrete classes.

keyIdea.title: How to Declare
keyIdea.text: Use interface to declare behaviors and implements to make a class adhere to those behaviors; implement all methods or declare the class abstract.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Declaring Interfaces
Declaration Pattern
Define method signatures and optional defaults
// Interface with default and static method
interface Flyable {
  void fly(); // implicitly public abstract

  default void takeOff() {
    System.out.println("Taking off...");
  }

  static void describeFlying() {
    System.out.println("Flyable objects can move through the air.");
  }
}

// Class implementing the interface
class Airplane implements Flyable {
  String model;
  public Airplane(String model) { this.model = model; }
  @Override
  public void fly() {
    System.out.println(model + " is soaring through the sky!");
  }
}
Notes
  • Methods in interfaces are public by default; implementations must be public.
  • Classes can implement multiple interfaces, separated by commas.
  • If a class doesn't implement all methods, it must be declared abstract.
Runtime Example
// Expected console output sequence
Taking off...
Boeing 747 is soaring through the sky!
Flyable objects can move through the air.

screens.title: Interface vs Abstract Class
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an interface and an abstract class depends on intent. Use an abstract class when you want to share implementation details and instance state between a family of classes: you can provide constructors, fields, and protected helper methods. By contrast, use an interface to express capabilities or behaviors that many otherwise unrelated classes might offer, where you do not need to share instance data. A key practical difference is multiple inheritance: a class can implement many interfaces but can only extend a single superclass. That makes interfaces ideal for composing orthogonal behaviors like Flyable and Swimmable. Another important point is evolution: prior to Java 8, interfaces were pure contracts; adding a method would break implementers. Default methods solved this by offering a safe default behavior. A common misconception is that interfaces are lighter and always better; if your design requires shared state or enforced constructor behavior, an abstract class is the correct choice. Exercise: when you see repeated fields and shared constructor logic across classes, prefer an abstract class; when you need composable abilities, prefer interfaces. Interface vs Abstract Class means abstract classes share state and implementation; interfaces define composable behaviors and allow multiple inheritance of type.. In practical terms, when to use each and common trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Interface vs Abstract Class
Abstract Class
  • Can hold instance fields and constructors.
  • Can provide concrete and abstract methods.
  • Single inheritance: a class extends one superclass.
  • Use when subclasses share state or common base behavior.
Misconception
Don't use abstract classes solely to group unrelated behaviors; that's what interfaces are for.
Interface
  • Defines method signatures and constants; Java 8+ supports default and static methods.
  • Enables multiple inheritance of type via implements.
  • Promotes loose coupling by depending on capability types.
  • Use when behavior is orthogonal and composable.
Design Tip
Prefer small, single-purpose interfaces. Compose behaviors instead of creating large catch-all interfaces.
Quick Check
If you need shared fields or common constructor logic, use an abstract class. If you need composable abilities across unrelated classes, use interfaces.

screens.title: Default Methods in Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Default methods were added to interfaces in Java 8 to allow interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementations. A default method provides a concrete implementation within an interface. Implementing classes may use that default behavior as-is or override it to supply specialized behavior. For example, Flyable can provide a default takeOff() that prints a generic message. Existing classes that implement Flyable will immediately inherit takeOff() without requiring changes. However, you must be careful: if two interfaces provide conflicting default methods and a class implements both, the class must resolve the conflict by overriding the method explicitly. Default methods are not a replacement for shared state or complex base behavior; they are a compatibility tool and a place for small, sensible defaults. Use them to provide common helper behavior that most implementers can accept. A practical example is adding a logging or simple setup method as a default. Misconception: default does not mean optional — the class still has the method, but it may use the interface's provided implementation unless it overrides it. Default Methods in Interfaces means default methods give interfaces a concrete method body so new behaviors can be added without breaking implementers; overrides resolve conflicts or customize behavior.. In practical terms, evolving interfaces safely with default implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Default Methods
keyIdea.text: Default methods give interfaces a concrete method body so new behaviors can be added without breaking implementers; overrides resolve conflicts or customize behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Default Methods
Why default methods?
Evolve interfaces and provide optional shared behavior.
interface Flyable {
  void fly();

  default void takeOff() {
    System.out.println("Taking off...");
  }
}

class Duck implements Flyable {
  String name;
  public Duck(String name) { this.name = name; }
  @Override
  public void fly() { System.out.println(name + " is flapping wings and flying!"); }
  // Duck may override takeOff() to customize behavior
}
Conflict Rules
If a class implements two interfaces that define the same default method, the class must override the method to resolve the conflict. This explicit decision prevents ambiguity.
Misconception
Default methods are not intended to replace base classes for shared mutable state or complex lifecycle behavior.
Practical Tip
Use default methods for small, reusable behavior like basic logging, a simple setup step, or backward-compatible conveniences.

screens.title: Static Methods in Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Static methods in interfaces are utility functions that belong to the interface type rather than to an implementing object. They are called on the interface name, for example Flyable. describeFlying(), and cannot be overridden by implementers. Use them to provide helper methods or factory-like utilities related to the interface's purpose. For instance, an interface describing printable content might include a static formatting helper. Static interface methods are useful because they keep related utilities next to the contract they serve, improving discoverability. A misconception is to try to access an interface's static method through an instance — static interface methods are not polymorphic and must be referenced by the interface name. Also, static methods do not carry state tied to instances. When designing, reserve static methods for utilities that have no dependency on a particular implementing class. The combination of default and static methods gives interfaces a richer toolbox: defaults provide per-instance fallbacks and static methods provide interface-scoped utilities. In practical terms, utilities that belong to the interface itself. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Static Methods
Interface Utilities
Static methods belong to the interface type itself
interface Flyable {
  void fly();

  static void describeFlying() {
    System.out.println("Flyable objects can move through the air.");
  }
}

// Call site
Flyable.describeFlying();
Guidelines
  • Use static methods for utilities related to the contract.
  • They cannot be overridden by implementers and are not polymorphic.
  • Keep static helpers side-effect free when possible.
Example Use
A Printable interface could expose a static format helper that all callers use before printing.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Duck & Airplane Demo
Code Walkthrough
interface Flyable {
  void fly();
  default void takeOff() { System.out.println("Taking off..."); }
  static void describeFlying() { System.out.println("Flyable objects can move through the air."); }
}

interface Swimmable { void swim(); }

class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable {
  String name;
  public Duck(String name) { this.name = name; }
  @Override
  public void fly() { System.out.println(name + " is flapping wings and flying!"); }
  @Override
  public void swim() { System.out.println(name + " is paddling and swimming!"); }
  @Override
  public void takeOff() { System.out.println(name + " is waddling, then launching into the air!"); }
}

class Airplane implements Flyable {
  String model;
  public Airplane(String model) { this.model = model; }
  @Override
  public void fly() { System.out.println(model + " is soaring through the sky!"); }
}

screens.title: When to Choose Interfaces — Practical Guidelines
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right abstraction reduces future refactoring. Start by asking: do you need to share instance state or constructor logic? If yes, prefer an abstract class. Do you want to express a capability that many unrelated classes might offer? If yes, prefer an interface. Keep interfaces small and focused — a single responsibility per interface makes them easier to compose. When you notice repeated utility behavior that applies across many implementers but does not require state, consider providing a default method. For cross-cutting helper code that is not instance-specific, put it in a static interface method or in a separate utility class. Another practical guideline: prefer interface types in public APIs and method signatures to decouple callers from implementations. A typical mistake is creating a large monolithic interface that forces classes to implement methods they don't need; instead split into smaller behavior-specific interfaces. Finally, when evolving a widely used interface, add default methods to preserve compatibility rather than changing the contract abruptly. These rules of thumb will keep your design flexible and maintainable. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: As you adopt interfaces, watch out for common mistakes that erode design quality. First, avoid large, catch-all interfaces that force classes to implement methods they do not need; this violates the interface segregation principle. Second, do not use interfaces to share mutable instance state. Interfaces do not support instance fields; putting shared state in an abstract class or composition object is the safer choice. Third, be cautious with default methods: they solve evolution problems but can create ambiguity if multiple interfaces offer the same default method; always resolve conflicts explicitly in the implementing class. Fourth, don't attempt to access static interface methods through instances; static methods belong to the interface type and should be invoked via the interface name. Fifth, remember visibility: methods implemented from interfaces must be public; narrowing visibility causes compile errors. Finally, resist making behavior choices based on implementation details; design APIs around minimal required behaviors. Recognizing and avoiding these pitfalls helps maintain clean, testable, and extensible systems. Common Mistakes
  • Creating fat interfaces that violate interface segregation; instead split by responsibility.
  • Using interfaces to try to share mutable instance state — use abstract classes or composition for shared fields.
  • Neglecting to explicitly resolve conflicting default methods when implementing multiple interfaces.
  • Trying to call static interface methods on instances — static methods are not polymorphic.
  • Implementing methods with reduced visibility; interface methods must be public in implementations.

Refactor fat interfaces into smaller ones, move shared state to a base class or composed helper, resolve default conflicts explicitly, and keep method visibility public.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we treat interfaces as formal contracts that describe what an object can do, not how it stores state. You'll learn how to declare an interface with the interface keyword and make classes adhere to that contract using implements. We'll look at how interfaces let a class belong to multiple type hierarchies, why that matters for loose coupling, and how Java 8 introduced default and static methods so interfaces can evolve safely. You will see concrete code examples: Flyable and Swimmable, a Duck class implementing both, and an Airplane implementing only Flyable. We'll also contrast interfaces with abstract classes so you can choose the right tool when designing systems. By the end you will understand when to define behaviors as interfaces, how default methods preserve compatibility, and how static interface methods offer utility behavior. Think of an interface as a promise: a class that signs it guarantees certain behaviors. Keep that promise clear and focused, and your codebase stays modular and easy to change.

These learning objectives guide what you will practice and why it matters. First, you'll be able to explain what an interface is in Java and how it acts as a contract for classes: that definition helps you design clear APIs and reason about capability-based types. Second, you'll use the interface keyword and implements clause to write interfaces and make concrete classes adhere to them; this skill is essential for building modular code and testing via mock implementations. Third, you'll distinguish interfaces from abstract classes: when to prefer behavior-focused interfaces versus inheritance-backed abstract classes that may carry shared state. Fourth, you will implement Java 8 features: default methods and static methods in interfaces, understanding how default methods allow you to evolve APIs without breaking existing implementers. Each objective ties directly to writing clearer, loosely coupled code that is easier to extend and maintain. Practice these in small examples and the printable-document activity to confirm mastery.

This second set of objectives focuses on applying interfaces in design and practice. You will build example classes that implement multiple interfaces, demonstrating multiple inheritance of type and how it enables polymorphism: a method can accept any object that satisfies an interface, regardless of its concrete class. You will implement default and static methods in interfaces and observe how a default method can be overridden when a class needs specialized behavior. You will practice the printable-document activity: define Printable, implement Report and Invoice, and iterate through an array of Printable objects to print polymorphically. Finally, you'll learn why interfaces promote loose coupling: code depends on capability types rather than concrete implementations, simplifying testing and extension. Each objective connects to writing maintainable, extensible systems where behavior is explicit and substitutable. Learning Objectives — Practice & Benefits means implement multiple interfaces, use polymorphism through interface types, and apply default/static methods in small tested examples.. In practical terms, apply interfaces for polymorphism, loose coupling, and multiple type inheritance. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An interface is a contract: it declares a set of method signatures that a class promises to implement. Unlike classes, interfaces are about behavior — 'can-do' — not about how data is stored. Historically, interfaces contained only abstract method signatures and public static final constants. That meant interfaces described what actions existed without any implementation detail. Understanding this distinction is crucial: when you design APIs, use interfaces to express capabilities other parts of your code can rely on, rather than tying them to a concrete implementation. A concrete example is a Flyable interface with void fly(). Any class—Duck, Airplane, Drone—that implements Flyable guarantees it can fly, and code can accept Flyable parameters without caring about the class behind it. A common misconception is to use interfaces to share state; interfaces do not hold instance state. If you need shared state or a partial implementation with fields, an abstract class may be appropriate. Takeaway: interfaces make behavior explicit and interchangeable; they simplify testing and extension by allowing substitution based on capability alone. Can you spot where a behavior belongs to an interface versus to a class with state?

Let's walk through how to declare an interface and make a class implement it. You use the interface keyword followed by method signatures. Implementing classes use implements and must provide concrete implementations for each abstract method. This pattern enables compile-time guarantees about available behaviors. As a concrete example, the Flyable interface declares void fly() and a default takeOff() in Java 8. A Duck class implements Flyable and Swimmable and supplies fly() and swim() method bodies; it can also override the default takeOff() to provide a specialized startup behavior. Note that fields declared in interfaces are implicitly public static final, so interfaces are not a place to put mutable instance fields. A common mistake is forgetting to add @Override annotations for implemented methods; while optional, they help catch signature mismatches at compile time. Practically, declare small focused interfaces for single responsibilities. Below you will find a code panel showing an interface, a class that implements it, and small runtime output to illustrate behavior. Use this pattern to document capabilities and enable polymorphic APIs that accept interface types rather than concrete classes.

Choosing between an interface and an abstract class depends on intent. Use an abstract class when you want to share implementation details and instance state between a family of classes: you can provide constructors, fields, and protected helper methods. By contrast, use an interface to express capabilities or behaviors that many otherwise unrelated classes might offer, where you do not need to share instance data. A key practical difference is multiple inheritance: a class can implement many interfaces but can only extend a single superclass. That makes interfaces ideal for composing orthogonal behaviors like Flyable and Swimmable. Another important point is evolution: prior to Java 8, interfaces were pure contracts; adding a method would break implementers. Default methods solved this by offering a safe default behavior. A common misconception is that interfaces are lighter and always better; if your design requires shared state or enforced constructor behavior, an abstract class is the correct choice. Exercise: when you see repeated fields and shared constructor logic across classes, prefer an abstract class; when you need composable abilities, prefer interfaces. Interface vs Abstract Class means abstract classes share state and implementation; interfaces define composable behaviors and allow multiple inheritance of type.. In practical terms, when to use each and common trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Default methods were added to interfaces in Java 8 to allow interfaces to evolve without breaking existing implementations. A default method provides a concrete implementation within an interface. Implementing classes may use that default behavior as-is or override it to supply specialized behavior. For example, Flyable can provide a default takeOff() that prints a generic message. Existing classes that implement Flyable will immediately inherit takeOff() without requiring changes. However, you must be careful: if two interfaces provide conflicting default methods and a class implements both, the class must resolve the conflict by overriding the method explicitly. Default methods are not a replacement for shared state or complex base behavior; they are a compatibility tool and a place for small, sensible defaults. Use them to provide common helper behavior that most implementers can accept. A practical example is adding a logging or simple setup method as a default. Misconception: default does not mean optional — the class still has the method, but it may use the interface's provided implementation unless it overrides it. Default Methods in Interfaces means default methods give interfaces a concrete method body so new behaviors can be added without breaking implementers; overrides resolve conflicts or customize behavior.. In practical terms, evolving interfaces safely with default implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Static methods in interfaces are utility functions that belong to the interface type rather than to an implementing object. They are called on the interface name, for example Flyable. describeFlying(), and cannot be overridden by implementers. Use them to provide helper methods or factory-like utilities related to the interface's purpose. For instance, an interface describing printable content might include a static formatting helper. Static interface methods are useful because they keep related utilities next to the contract they serve, improving discoverability. A misconception is to try to access an interface's static method through an instance — static interface methods are not polymorphic and must be referenced by the interface name. Also, static methods do not carry state tied to instances. When designing, reserve static methods for utilities that have no dependency on a particular implementing class. The combination of default and static methods gives interfaces a richer toolbox: defaults provide per-instance fallbacks and static methods provide interface-scoped utilities. When a method accepts a Flyable parameter, it can work with Airplane, Duck, Drone, or any object that implements Flyable. Choosing the right abstraction reduces future refactoring. Start by asking: do you need to share instance state or constructor logic? If yes, prefer an abstract class. Do you want to express a capability that many unrelated classes might offer? If yes, prefer an interface. When you notice repeated utility behavior that applies across many implementers but does not require state, consider providing a default method. For cross-cutting helper code that is not instance-specific, put it in a static interface method or in a separate utility class. As you adopt interfaces, watch out for common mistakes that erode design quality. First, avoid large, catch-all interfaces that force classes to implement methods they do not need; this violates the interface segregation principle. Second, do not use interfaces to share mutable instance state. Interfaces do not support instance fields; putting shared state in an abstract class or composition object is the safer choice. Third, be cautious with default methods: they solve evolution problems but can create ambiguity if multiple interfaces offer the same default method; always resolve conflicts explicitly in the implementing class. Fourth, don't attempt to access static interface methods through instances; static methods belong to the interface type and should be invoked via the interface name. Fifth, remember visibility: methods implemented from interfaces must be public; narrowing visibility causes compile errors. Finally, resist making behavior choices based on implementation details; design APIs around minimal required behaviors. Recognizing and avoiding these pitfalls helps maintain clean, testable, and extensible systems. Here are three compact concepts to anchor your understanding. First, the Interface: a contract of behaviors, historically abstract, and now capable of default and static methods so APIs can evolve. Second, Default Method: a concrete method inside an interface that offers a default behavior so implementers remain compatible when new behaviors are added. Third, Multiple Inheritance of Type: a class can implement several interfaces, composing capabilities without inheriting state. Use these concepts as quick checks when designing: express capabilities with interfaces, use defaults for safe evolution, and leverage multiple interfaces for composable behaviors.
